## **Lucky loonie mintage plunges to record low in 2013**

**A review of mintage figures for 2013 suggests that some modern coins may prove difficult to find.**

While collectors often await the mintage figures in the Royal Canadian Mint’s (RCM) annual report, this year, Canadian Coin News looked at the figures over the past 10 years, and found that 2013 could be a year to watch in some denominations. Of particular interest are the higher value $1 and $2 coins, produced before the composition and design change introduced partway through 2012. For instance a 2013-dated $2 coin or a lucky loonie may be harder to find than that elusive de Salaberry 25-cent piece. Mintages for that year were updated in the 2013 report.

The RCM’s report did explain that mintages for last year were down from the previous year, and in most cases the drop was substantial.

The higher value coins saw a slight change in composition during the year to accommodate the RCM’s new plating plant, while at the same time new micro-engraving features were added including edge lettering the $2 coin.

The number of original pattern $2 coins produced in 2012 was a mere 1,531,000, down from 22,488,000 the year before, and the lowest reported in the last decade. It was also the last year for that composition. The new type $2 may be a tough find with the 2013 date, just 12,390,000 were produced, compared to 82,862,000 new-style coins produced in 2012. In the previous decade the lowest mintage was 22,488,000 in 2011 and the highest was 38,957,000 in 2007.

There is more balance in the case of the $1 coin. In 2012 the RCM manufactured just 2,414,000 old-pattern coins and 107,105,000 new-pattern coins. In 2013 a further 120,330,000 new-style loonies were struck. The lucky loonie struck in 2013 had it lowest mintage ever, just 969,000; the lowest mintage ever for the circulating coin. In the last 10 years the highest loonie mintage was 38,048,000 in 2007 and 20,410,000 in 2011.

High mintage figures for $1 and $2 coins in 2013 were expected, as the RCM’s alloy recovery program was culling the older composition coins out of circulation during the year.

The number of 50-cent coins produced, almost entirely for the collector market, was up in 2013 to 375,000 compared to 250,000 the year before. In 2010, the lowest year in the survey period, the mintage was 150,000.

Caribou pattern 25-cent pieces also saw a lower than usual mintage. In 2013 a total of 68,498,000 coins were produced, compared to 153,450,000 the year before. A further 12,500,000 each of the de Salaberry and Laura Secord coins were struck in 2013. The highest number in the past 10 years for the Caribou 25-centwas a whopping 423,189,999 in 2008, while the lowest was 20,446,000 in 2009.

The 2013-dated 10-cent coins set a new 10-year record, with just 104,775,000 compared to 334,675,000 in 2012. The highest in the period was 467,495,000 in 2008.

The humble five-cent coin, now the lowest-value coin in production, may be another tough find, with another record low posted in 2013. Last year just 78,120,000 nickels were produced, the lowest recorded since the coin shifted to a plated composition. The cupro-nickel version of the coin did see a lower mintage of 43,008,000 in 2008. Those coins were an irregularity, produced long after the RCM had shifted to plated coins, in order to compensate for a supply shortage of tri-plated blanks for five-cent coins.

Although not produced in 2013, the updated figures in the report show that 87,972,000 copper-plated zinc pennies were made in 2012, the lowest recorded over the past decade. The highest was 30,525,000 in 2005. The copper-plated steel coins were much more common. In 2012 a total of 111,375,000 were produced, the lowest figure in the past 10 years. The highest mintage was reported at 1,062,275 in 2006.

The total number of coins produced does not tell whole story of Canadian circulating coins.

Once made in Winnipeg, coins are shipped to 12 coin distribution centres across Canada based on local demand. Once in a centre, coins are then shipped to financial institutions or directly to high-volume users.

In the previous year, all coin centres ordered some inventories of each circulating coins, but some ordered relatively small numbers, making those coins harder to find in some parts of the country than in others.

The lowest demands were: five cent, St. Johns, N.L., 318,000; 10 cents, Quebec City, Que., 2,000; 25 cents, Halifax, N.S., 594,000; $1, St. John, N.B., 86,000; and $1, Halifax, 165,000.

The RCM distribution report simply records the number of coins shipped in a calendar year, and does not make any record on the commemorative designs or the years on the coins, so the distribution numbers can only be used as relative guides.

All circulating coin numbers in RCM annual reports are rounded to the nearest thousand.

## Recent Years Show Some Low Mintage Canadian Coins

## **Lucky loonie mintage plunges to record low in 2013**

**A review of mintage figures for 2013 suggests that some modern coins may prove difficult to find.**

While collectors often await the mintage figures in the Royal Canadian Mint’s (RCM) annual report, this year, Canadian Coin News looked at the figures over the past 10 years, and found that 2013 could be a year to watch in some denominations. Of particular interest are the higher value $1 and $2 coins, produced before the composition and design change introduced partway through 2012. For instance a 2013-dated $2 coin or a lucky loonie may be harder to find than that elusive de Salaberry 25-cent piece. Mintages for that year were updated in the 2013 report.

The RCM’s report did explain that mintages for last year were down from the previous year, and in most cases the drop was substantial.

The higher value coins saw a slight change in composition during the year to accommodate the RCM’s new plating plant, while at the same time new micro-engraving features were added including edge lettering the $2 coin.

The number of original pattern $2 coins produced in 2012 was a mere 1,531,000, down from 22,488,000 the year before, and the lowest reported in the last decade. It was also the last year for that composition. The new type $2 may be a tough find with the 2013 date, just 12,390,000 were produced, compared to 82,862,000 new-style coins produced in 2012. In the previous decade the lowest mintage was 22,488,000 in 2011 and the highest was 38,957,000 in 2007.

There is more balance in the case of the $1 coin. In 2012 the RCM manufactured just 2,414,000 old-pattern coins and 107,105,000 new-pattern coins. In 2013 a further 120,330,000 new-style loonies were struck. The lucky loonie struck in 2013 had it lowest mintage ever, just 969,000; the lowest mintage ever for the circulating coin. In the last 10 years the highest loonie mintage was 38,048,000 in 2007 and 20,410,000 in 2011.

High mintage figures for $1 and $2 coins in 2013 were expected, as the RCM’s alloy recovery program was culling the older composition coins out of circulation during the year.

The number of 50-cent coins produced, almost entirely for the collector market, was up in 2013 to 375,000 compared to 250,000 the year before. In 2010, the lowest year in the survey period, the mintage was 150,000.

Caribou pattern 25-cent pieces also saw a lower than usual mintage. In 2013 a total of 68,498,000 coins were produced, compared to 153,450,000 the year before. A further 12,500,000 each of the de Salaberry and Laura Secord coins were struck in 2013. The highest number in the past 10 years for the Caribou 25-centwas a whopping 423,189,999 in 2008, while the lowest was 20,446,000 in 2009.

The 2013-dated 10-cent coins set a new 10-year record, with just 104,775,000 compared to 334,675,000 in 2012. The highest in the period was 467,495,000 in 2008.

The humble five-cent coin, now the lowest-value coin in production, may be another tough find, with another record low posted in 2013. Last year just 78,120,000 nickels were produced, the lowest recorded since the coin shifted to a plated composition. The cupro-nickel version of the coin did see a lower mintage of 43,008,000 in 2008. Those coins were an irregularity, produced long after the RCM had shifted to plated coins, in order to compensate for a supply shortage of tri-plated blanks for five-cent coins.

Although not produced in 2013, the updated figures in the report show that 87,972,000 copper-plated zinc pennies were made in 2012, the lowest recorded over the past decade. The highest was 30,525,000 in 2005. The copper-plated steel coins were much more common. In 2012 a total of 111,375,000 were produced, the lowest figure in the past 10 years. The highest mintage was reported at 1,062,275 in 2006.

The total number of coins produced does not tell whole story of Canadian circulating coins.

Once made in Winnipeg, coins are shipped to 12 coin distribution centres across Canada based on local demand. Once in a centre, coins are then shipped to financial institutions or directly to high-volume users.

In the previous year, all coin centres ordered some inventories of each circulating coins, but some ordered relatively small numbers, making those coins harder to find in some parts of the country than in others.

The lowest demands were: five cent, St. Johns, N.L., 318,000; 10 cents, Quebec City, Que., 2,000; 25 cents, Halifax, N.S., 594,000; $1, St. John, N.B., 86,000; and $1, Halifax, 165,000.

The RCM distribution report simply records the number of coins shipped in a calendar year, and does not make any record on the commemorative designs or the years on the coins, so the distribution numbers can only be used as relative guides.

All circulating coin numbers in RCM annual reports are rounded to the nearest thousand.

# 2013 Gold and Silver Kilo Coins Depict Canada’s Arctic Landscape

By

[Darrin Lee Unser](https://www.coinnews.net/author/darrinluaolcom/)

 -

January 17, 2013

0

The Royal Canadian Mint expands on a frigid glacial theme this year with the release of two new coins — Canada’s Arctic Landscape 1 Kilo Fine Gold Coin and Canada’s Arctic Landscape 1 Kilo Fine Silver Coin.

[![Image 3: 2013 Canada's Arctic Landscape Gold and Silver Kilo Coins](http://www.coinnews.net/wp-content/uploads/2013/01/2013-Canadas-Arctic-Landscape-Gold-and-Silver-Kilo-Coins-510x254.jpg)](http://www.coinnews.net/wp-content/uploads/2013/01/2013-Canadas-Arctic-Landscape-Gold-and-Silver-Kilo-Coins.jpg)

2013 Canadas Arctic Landscape Gold and Silver Kilo Coins

Both kilo coins contain the same basic obverse and reverse imagery. One is in 99.99% pure gold and the other is in 99.99% pure silver. Each is in proof quality with extremely limited mintages.

> "Locked in twilight for much of the year, cast in blinding contrast for its few months of midnight sun, the Canadian Arctic is like no other place on Earth," states the Royal Canadian Mint on the coin’s product pages.
> 
> 
> "For Canadians, the Arctic represents not only a massive component of the nation’s geography and the interconnectedness of Canadian lands from sea to sea to sea, but the source of the ice, snow and cold that has carved out not only the land but the soul of this country."

**Canada’s Arctic Landscape Kilo Coin Designs and Specifications**

Shown on the reverse of the gold and silver kilo coins is a design by Canadian artist W. David Ward. It offers a detailed scene of the north shore of Baffin Island overlooking Lancaster Sound at the mouth of the Northwest Passage. Indicative of Canada’s entire Arctic region, the design includes icebergs and frozen waters. Off in the distance, glacier topped mountains appear on the horizon. Inscribed toward the top is CANADA while the artist’s initials are found near the bottom.

[![Image 4: 2013](http://www.coinnews.net/wp-content/uploads/2013/01/2013-2500-Canadas-Arctic-Landscape-1-Kilo-Gold-Coin-300x286.jpg)](http://www.coinnews.net/wp-content/uploads/2013/01/2013-2500-Canadas-Arctic-Landscape-1-Kilo-Gold-Coin.jpg)

2013 $2500 Canadas Arctic Landscape 1 Kilo Gold Coin

The obverse of the kilo coins feature Susanna Blunt’s effigy of Queen Elizabeth II. Surrounding the portrait are the inscriptions of ELIZABETH II, D G REGINA, and 2013. In addition, shown are legal tender face values of 2500 DOLLARS for the gold kilo coin and 250 DOLLARS for the silver kilo coin.

Each proof quality coin features a weight of 1,000 grams and a serrated edge. The 99.99% pure gold coin has a diameter of 101.6 mm while the 99.99% pure silver coin’s diameter is 101.8 mm. These coins ship within a custom maple wood box lined with flock.

[![Image 5: 2013 0 Canada's Arctic Landscape 1 Kilo Silver Coin](http://www.coinnews.net/wp-content/uploads/2013/01/2013-250-Canadas-Arctic-Landscape-1-Kilo-Silver-Coin-300x286.jpg)](http://www.coinnews.net/wp-content/uploads/2013/01/2013-250-Canadas-Arctic-Landscape-1-Kilo-Silver-Coin.jpg)

2013 $250 Canadas Arctic Landscape 1 Kilo Silver Coin

The 2013 Canada’s Arctic Landscape 1 Kilo Gold Coin has a maximum limit of 20 pieces. The price is CAD $69,000.00. The 2013 Canada’s Arctic Landscape 1 Kilo Silver Coin features a mintage of 750 with pricing of CAD $2,249.95.

Order these kilo coins directly from the Mint at 1-800-267-1871 in Canada, 1-800-268-6468 in the US, or on the Internet at [www.mint.ca](http://www.mint.ca/ "www.mint.ca").

**About the Royal Canadian Mint**

The Royal Canadian Mint is the Crown Corporation responsible for the minting and distribution of Canada’s circulation coins. An ISO 9001-2008 certified company, the Mint is one of the largest and most versatile mints in the world, offering a range of specialized, high quality coinage products and related services on an international scale.

## 25 cents 2013

[![Image 3: 25 cents 2013 - Canadian coin](https://www.numicanada.com/medias/pieces-de-monnaie/valeur/25-cents-2013-canada-coin-twenty-five-cent-canadian-coins-quarter.jpg)](https://www.numicanada.com/medias/pieces-de-monnaie/valeur/25-cents-2013-canada-coin-twenty-five-cent-canadian-coins-quarter.jpg "25 cents 2013 - Canadian coin")

100 years after Canadian Prime Minister Sir Robert Borden despatched explorers and researchers from Victoria, British Columbia, on a mission to map the Canada's Western Arctic and study its peoples, wildlife and geology, the Royal Canadian Mint released two circulated 25 cents coins. The coins were unveiled in Victoria and in Cambridge Bay, Nunavut. [Read more »](https://www.coinsandcanada.com/coins-articles.php?article=100-years-of-canadian-arctic-expedition-coins-of-2013&id=1005 "100 years of Canadian Arctic Expedition - Coins of 2013")

The War of 1812 paved the way for Confederation. It was the fight for Canada and a defining moment in our country's history that saw British regular forces, English and French-speaking militia, First Nations and Métis allies join together to defend the borders. Without their courage and sacrifice, Canada as we know it would not exist. 2013 was a busy and exciting year for Canada and the rest of the world! According to Chinese astrology, 2013 was the year of the snake; specifically, the water snake. ### **The Birth Of Prince George**

On July 22, 2013, the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge welcomed their first child, Prince George, into the world. The Royal Canadian Mint created a unique and spectacular coin worthy of commemorating that joyous occasion: the[2013 Canada $5 Royal Infant Toys Fine Silver](https://colonialacrescoins.myshopify.com/products/2013-canada-5-royal-infant-toys-fine-silver-no-tax?_pos=1&_psq=2013+CANADA+%245+ROYAL+INFANT+TOYS+FINE+SILVER+%28NO+TAX%29&_ss=e&_v=1.0)coin. Expertly crafted of 99.99% pure silver, the coin celebrates the new prince as well as the Royal Family’s special relationship with Canada.

Ornately detailed symbols of babyhood, such as rattles, sippy cups, bibs, and tiny shoes, form a ring around the coin, representing the whirlwind experience of the newborn phase. In the centre of the ring are the Royal Couple’s ciphers, accented with 24 karat gold and flanked by a pair of symbolic maple leaves. This stunning coin is an excellent way to celebrate the arrival of Prince George or any special 2013 baby.

### **Chinese Year Of The Snake**

Chinese astrologers regard the snake as the most refined and intuitive animal sign. People born in the year of the snake are thought to be intelligent, calm, reflective, and hard workers. They tend to be lucky, especially with finances, so what better way to commemorate someone born in 2013 than with a 99.99% pure silver[2013 Canada $10 Year of the Snake](https://colonialacrescoins.myshopify.com/products/2013-canada-10-year-of-the-snake-1-2oz-fine-silver-coin-no-tax?_pos=1&_psq=2013+CANADA+%2410+YEAR+OF+THE+SNAKE+1%2F2OZ.+FINE+SILVER+COIN+%28NO+TAX%29&_ss=e&_v=1.0)coin?

While Chinese astrology includes several types of snakes, 2013 was the year of the water snake, as symbolized by the delicately curled waves in the coin’s intriguing design by Canadian artist Aries Cheung. Those born under the water snake sign are especially sociable and are excellent leaders. This beautiful coin would make a wonderful gift for anyone born in 2013.

2013 was a busy and exciting year for Canada and the rest of the world! ### **The Birth Of Prince George**

On July 22, 2013, the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge welcomed their first child, Prince George, into the world. The Royal Canadian Mint created a unique and spectacular coin worthy of commemorating that joyous occasion: the[2013 Canada $5 Royal Infant Toys Fine Silver](https://colonialacrescoins.myshopify.com/products/2013-canada-5-royal-infant-toys-fine-silver-no-tax?_pos=1&_psq=2013+CANADA+%245+ROYAL+INFANT+TOYS+FINE+SILVER+%28NO+TAX%29&_ss=e&_v=1.0)coin. Expertly crafted of 99.99% pure silver, the coin celebrates the new prince as well as the Royal Family’s special relationship with Canada.

Ornately detailed symbols of babyhood, such as rattles, sippy cups, bibs, and tiny shoes, form a ring around the coin, representing the whirlwind experience of the newborn phase. In the centre of the ring are the Royal Couple’s ciphers, accented with 24 karat gold and flanked by a pair of symbolic maple leaves. This stunning coin is an excellent way to celebrate the arrival of Prince George or any special 2013 baby.

### **Chinese Year Of The Snake**

Chinese astrologers regard the snake as the most refined and intuitive animal sign. People born in the year of the snake are thought to be intelligent, calm, reflective, and hard workers. They tend to be lucky, especially with finances, so what better way to commemorate someone born in 2013 than with a 99.99% pure silver[2013 Canada $10 Year of the Snake](https://colonialacrescoins.myshopify.com/products/2013-canada-10-year-of-the-snake-1-2oz-fine-silver-coin-no-tax?_pos=1&_psq=2013+CANADA+%2410+YEAR+OF+THE+SNAKE+1%2F2OZ.+FINE+SILVER+COIN+%28NO+TAX%29&_ss=e&_v=1.0)coin?

While Chinese astrology includes several types of snakes, 2013 was the year of the water snake, as symbolized by the delicately curled waves in the coin’s intriguing design by Canadian artist Aries Cheung. Those born under the water snake sign are especially sociable and are excellent leaders. This beautiful coin would make a wonderful gift for anyone born in 2013.

# 1 dollar

### **Striking in its Solitude – the 1‑dollar Coin, familiarly known as the 'loonie'**

The 1-dollar circulation coin was introduced in 1987 as a cost-saving measure to replace the one-dollar bill. The coin was instantly dubbed the 'loonie' after the solitary loon that graces the coin's reverse side. The nickname caught on and Canadians have been using it ever since. The loon design was created by noted wildlife artist Robert-Ralph Carmichael.

## Reverse Side Designs

### Reverse Side Designs

###### 1935 – 1938, 1940 – 1948, 1950 – 1957, 1959 – 1963, 1965 – 1966, 1968 – 1969, and 1975 – 1986

The Voyageur

This design by Emanuel Hahn features a voyageur and his Indigenous guide travelling by canoe. The illustration has been modified only slightly over the years.

###### 1939

The Royal Visit

This design by Emanuel Hahn commemorates the visit of His Majesty King George VI and Queen Elizabeth to Ottawa. The Latin phrase "Fide Quorum Regnat" means "He reigns by the faith of his people."

###### 1949

Newfoundland joins Confederation

Thomas Shingles' design commemorates Newfoundland's status as a province of Canada. Pictured on the coin is the _Matthew_, the ship historians believe John Cabot was sailing when he landed in Newfoundland in 1497. Below the ship reads the Latin inscription "Floreat Terra Nova," meaning: "May the New Found Land Flourish."

###### 1958

The founding of British Columbia

Stephen Trenka's representation of a mortuary pole with the Rocky Mountain backdrop marks the centenary of both the Cariboo Gold Rush and the creation of British Columbia as a colony of England.

###### 1964

The Confederation meetings

Thomas Shingles' design features the French fleur-de-lis, the Irish shamrock, the Scottish thistle, and the English rose. It commemorates the 100th anniversary of the Charlottetown and Quebec City meetings that led to Confederation.

###### 1967

The centennial dollar

Alex Colville created a special set of coin designs to commemorate the 100th anniversary of Canadian Confederation; the 1-dollar coin features a Canada goose.

###### 1970

Manitoba's centennial

Raymond Taylor's prairie crocus design commemorates the centennial of Manitoba joining Confederation.

###### 1971

British Columbia's centennial

Thomas Shingles' design commemorates the centennial of British Columbia's joining Confederation. The coin features British Columbia's coat of arms and its provincial flower, the dogwood.

###### 1973

Prince Edward Island's centennial

Walter Ott's rendering of P.E.I.'s Provincial Legislature building commemorates the centennial of the province's accession to Canada.

###### 1974

Winnipeg's centennial

Patrick Brindley created this design from a drawing by Paul Pederson to commemorate Winnipeg's centennial anniversary. Inside the two zeroes of '"00" are images of Winnipeg's Main street in 1874 (left) and 1974 (right).

###### 1982

The Constitution commemorative coin

This design features the famous painting of the Fathers of Confederation along with the inscriptions "Confederation 1867" and "Constitution 1982."

###### 1984

Jacques Cartier on the Gaspé

Hector Greville's design of Jacques Cartier and a cross with the French coat of arms commemorates the 450th anniversary of the explorer's landing on the Gaspé Peninsula.

###### 1987 – 1991, 1993 – present

The Loonie

The 1-dollar bill was replaced in 1987 by a new eleven-sided circulation coin nicknamed the 'Loonie'. Robert-Ralph Carmichael's popular design features a Canadian loon, and is made of aureate bronze.

###### 1992

The 125th Anniversary of Confederation

Rita Swanson's design features three children with a Canadian flag on Parliament Hill in commemoration of Canada's 125th birthday. Note the clock on the Peace Tower reads 1:25.

###### 1994

The National War Memorial coin

A representation of the National War Memorial in Ottawa honours the contribution and sacrifice made by Canadian soldiers in both World Wars and the Korean War.

###### 1995

The Peacekeeping coin

This coin commemorates the 50th anniversary of the United Nations, and pays tribute to the Canadians who have served as UN peacekeepers. It features an image of the Peacekeeping Monument in Ottawa.

###### 2004

Lucky Loonie

The 2004 Lucky Loonie features the common loon design accompanied by the Canadian Olympic logo.

###### 2005

Terry Fox

The Terry Fox coin commemorates the 25th Anniversary of the Marathon of Hope. This coin was designed by Stan Witten.

###### 2006

Lucky Loonie

This coin, which features the familiar loon in flight along with the official emblem of the Canadian Olympic Team, serves as a good luck charm for Canadian athletes served at the 2006 Olympic and Paralympic Winter Games.

###### 2008

Lucky Loonie

The 2008 Lucky Loonie features a common Loon getting ready to take flight with the Canadian Olympic Team's logo at its side. The Mint provided each member of the Canadian Olympic and Paralympic Teams competing in Beijing with a Lucky Loonie as their own personal good luck charm.

# 1 dollar

### **Striking in its Solitude – the 1‑dollar Coin, familiarly known as the 'loonie'**

The 1-dollar circulation coin was introduced in 1987 as a cost-saving measure to replace the one-dollar bill. The coin was instantly dubbed the 'loonie' after the solitary loon that graces the coin's reverse side. The nickname caught on and Canadians have been using it ever since. The loon design was created by noted wildlife artist Robert-Ralph Carmichael.

## Reverse Side Designs

### Reverse Side Designs

###### 1935 – 1938, 1940 – 1948, 1950 – 1957, 1959 – 1963, 1965 – 1966, 1968 – 1969, and 1975 – 1986

The Voyageur

This design by Emanuel Hahn features a voyageur and his Indigenous guide travelling by canoe. The illustration has been modified only slightly over the years.

###### 1939

The Royal Visit

This design by Emanuel Hahn commemorates the visit of His Majesty King George VI and Queen Elizabeth to Ottawa. The Latin phrase "Fide Quorum Regnat" means "He reigns by the faith of his people."

###### 1949

Newfoundland joins Confederation

Thomas Shingles' design commemorates Newfoundland's status as a province of Canada. Pictured on the coin is the _Matthew_, the ship historians believe John Cabot was sailing when he landed in Newfoundland in 1497. Below the ship reads the Latin inscription "Floreat Terra Nova," meaning: "May the New Found Land Flourish."

###### 1958

The founding of British Columbia

Stephen Trenka's representation of a mortuary pole with the Rocky Mountain backdrop marks the centenary of both the Cariboo Gold Rush and the creation of British Columbia as a colony of England.

###### 1964

The Confederation meetings

Thomas Shingles' design features the French fleur-de-lis, the Irish shamrock, the Scottish thistle, and the English rose. It commemorates the 100th anniversary of the Charlottetown and Quebec City meetings that led to Confederation.

###### 1967

The centennial dollar

Alex Colville created a special set of coin designs to commemorate the 100th anniversary of Canadian Confederation; the 1-dollar coin features a Canada goose.

###### 1970

Manitoba's centennial

Raymond Taylor's prairie crocus design commemorates the centennial of Manitoba joining Confederation.

###### 1971

British Columbia's centennial

Thomas Shingles' design commemorates the centennial of British Columbia's joining Confederation. The coin features British Columbia's coat of arms and its provincial flower, the dogwood.

###### 1973

Prince Edward Island's centennial

Walter Ott's rendering of P.E.I.'s Provincial Legislature building commemorates the centennial of the province's accession to Canada.

###### 1974

Winnipeg's centennial

Patrick Brindley created this design from a drawing by Paul Pederson to commemorate Winnipeg's centennial anniversary. Inside the two zeroes of '"00" are images of Winnipeg's Main street in 1874 (left) and 1974 (right).

###### 1982

The Constitution commemorative coin

This design features the famous painting of the Fathers of Confederation along with the inscriptions "Confederation 1867" and "Constitution 1982."

###### 1984

Jacques Cartier on the Gaspé

Hector Greville's design of Jacques Cartier and a cross with the French coat of arms commemorates the 450th anniversary of the explorer's landing on the Gaspé Peninsula.

###### 1987 – 1991, 1993 – present

The Loonie

The 1-dollar bill was replaced in 1987 by a new eleven-sided circulation coin nicknamed the 'Loonie'. Robert-Ralph Carmichael's popular design features a Canadian loon, and is made of aureate bronze.

###### 1992

The 125th Anniversary of Confederation

Rita Swanson's design features three children with a Canadian flag on Parliament Hill in commemoration of Canada's 125th birthday. Note the clock on the Peace Tower reads 1:25.

###### 1994

The National War Memorial coin

A representation of the National War Memorial in Ottawa honours the contribution and sacrifice made by Canadian soldiers in both World Wars and the Korean War.

###### 1995

The Peacekeeping coin

This coin commemorates the 50th anniversary of the United Nations, and pays tribute to the Canadians who have served as UN peacekeepers. It features an image of the Peacekeeping Monument in Ottawa.

###### 2004

Lucky Loonie

The 2004 Lucky Loonie features the common loon design accompanied by the Canadian Olympic logo.

###### 2005

Terry Fox

The Terry Fox coin commemorates the 25th Anniversary of the Marathon of Hope. This coin was designed by Stan Witten.

###### 2006

Lucky Loonie

This coin, which features the familiar loon in flight along with the official emblem of the Canadian Olympic Team, serves as a good luck charm for Canadian athletes served at the 2006 Olympic and Paralympic Winter Games.

###### 2008

Lucky Loonie

The 2008 Lucky Loonie features a common Loon getting ready to take flight with the Canadian Olympic Team's logo at its side. The Mint provided each member of the Canadian Olympic and Paralympic Teams competing in Beijing with a Lucky Loonie as their own personal good luck charm.

# Canadian sets have doubled die Loon dollar

*   By [Jeff Starck](https://www.coinworld.com/authors/jeff-starck.html)
  
*    Published: Sep 1, 2013, 8 PM 

![Image 5: 2013_uncirculated_set_packaging_1](https://www.coinworld.com/images/default-source/news/2013_uncirculated_set_packaging_1.tmb-slide-1900.jpg?Culture=en&sfvrsn=7bc663f4_0)

 The Royal Canadian Mint has not provided an estimate of how many doubled die coins may exist, but the maximum mintage of Canada’s annual Uncirculated set is 75,000 sets. 
Image courtesy of [www.mint.ca](http://www.mint.ca/).

![Image 6: loon_merged_1](https://www.coinworld.com/images/default-source/news/loon_merged_1.tmb-slide-1900.jpg?Culture=en&sfvrsn=ff65488b_0)

 Dollar coins in Canada’s annual Uncirculated collector set have been found with visible doubling on the reverse, representing Class IV Offset Hub Doubling, most visible in the words CANADA and DOLLAR. 
Coin World images by Ray Wilder; set loaned for photography by Gatewest Coins.

![Image 7: 2-dollar_merged](https://www.coinworld.com/images/default-source/news/2-dollar_merged.tmb-slide-1900.jpg?Culture=en&sfvrsn=12b0900a_0)

 Examples of doubling on the obverse of Canada’s $2 coin have also been discovered in the annual Uncirculated set. 
Coin World images by Ray Wilder; set loaned for photography by Gatewest Coins.

Previous

Next

Some collectors who bought Canada’s annual 2013 Uncirculated set are being doubly rewarded with die varieties.

An unknown number of sets feature examples of Loon dollars with a doubled die reverse, and some of those same sets also feature Polar Bear $2 coins with a doubled die obverse.

Dollar coin doubling

While the coin has not been certified by any grading service, _Coin World_ has physically examined an example of the set containing the error. _Coin World_ News Editor William T. Gibbs identified the Loon dollar as probably showing Class IV Offset Hub Doubling. _Coin World’s_ Varieties Notebook columnist John Wexler agreed with that conclusion, after inspecting a digital image of the coin.

The Loon dollar exhibits doubling that is shifted in the same direction, the identifying characteristic of Class IV Offset Hub Doubling, which means the hub to die alignment was offset to one side. This type of doubling can occur with single-press hubbing, which was first used for Canadian coins in 1978.

Doubling is perhaps most visible in the words CANADA and DOLLAR and the designer’s initials on the reverse of the coin, which displays the standard Loon dollar design by Robert Ralph-Carmichael.

Trees at the water’s edge also exhibit doubling, and doubling is seen at the left wall of the incuse circle in which the maple leaf security device is found.

Wexler initially believed the doubling on the Loon dollar to be mechanical doubling, but closer inspection “shows a strong notching effect on many of the letters. The doubling on the beads near the rim does appear to be raised and rounded as does the doubling on other fine details such as the small trees and the designer’s initials.”

The final initial in the designer’s initials shows very nice separation of images, he added.

Class I doubling, like that on the famous 1955 Lincoln, Doubled Die Obverse cent, would give a notably different appearance than what is seen on the Loon dollar in the set.

Doubling on $2 coin

Less severe doubling is visible on the $2 coin, especially so in the word ELIZABETH, the year 2013 and the designer’s initials on the shoulder of Susanna Blunt’s effigy of Queen Elizabeth II.

The class of doubling on the $2 coin appears to be the same as on the Loon dollar, Wexler said.

The two coins illustrated with this article are in the same sealed set sold by the Royal Canadian Mint.

Discovery, RCM response

Variety collectors and some Canadian collectors first noticed the doubling back in March, based on online collector forum postings.

Cameron Giesbrecht, director of numismatics at Winnipeg’s Gatewest Coins, alerted _Coin World_ on Aug. 16, a few weeks after an unnamed customer of Gatewest tipped him off about the doubling.

Christine Aquino, director of communications at the Royal Canadian Mint, said the RCM was not aware of the doubling on the coins in the Uncirculated sets, though there was a general “understanding that this is a defect that can occur from time to time.”

The RCM has not located the die or dies responsible for striking the doubled coins, and could not provide an estimate of the possible numbers of pieces produced and released.

The set has a maximum mintage of 75,000 sets. Examples of the sets remained available Aug. 29 through the RCM website for the official issue price of $24.95 Canadian.

Examples of the Loon dollar with the doubling have sold through auction site [www.ebay.com](http://www.ebay.com/) for between $25 and $30, a price that die variety specialist Wexler noted was “quite a bargain” for such a “major variety.” ¦

# Canadian sets have doubled die Loon dollar

*   By [Jeff Starck](https://www.coinworld.com/authors/jeff-starck.html)
  
*    Published: Sep 1, 2013, 8 PM 

![Image 5: 2013_uncirculated_set_packaging_1](https://www.coinworld.com/images/default-source/news/2013_uncirculated_set_packaging_1.tmb-slide-1900.jpg?Culture=en&sfvrsn=7bc663f4_0)

 The Royal Canadian Mint has not provided an estimate of how many doubled die coins may exist, but the maximum mintage of Canada’s annual Uncirculated set is 75,000 sets. 
Image courtesy of [www.mint.ca](http://www.mint.ca/).

![Image 6: loon_merged_1](https://www.coinworld.com/images/default-source/news/loon_merged_1.tmb-slide-1900.jpg?Culture=en&sfvrsn=ff65488b_0)

 Dollar coins in Canada’s annual Uncirculated collector set have been found with visible doubling on the reverse, representing Class IV Offset Hub Doubling, most visible in the words CANADA and DOLLAR. 
Coin World images by Ray Wilder; set loaned for photography by Gatewest Coins.

![Image 7: 2-dollar_merged](https://www.coinworld.com/images/default-source/news/2-dollar_merged.tmb-slide-1900.jpg?Culture=en&sfvrsn=12b0900a_0)

 Examples of doubling on the obverse of Canada’s $2 coin have also been discovered in the annual Uncirculated set. 
Coin World images by Ray Wilder; set loaned for photography by Gatewest Coins.

Previous

Next

Some collectors who bought Canada’s annual 2013 Uncirculated set are being doubly rewarded with die varieties.

An unknown number of sets feature examples of Loon dollars with a doubled die reverse, and some of those same sets also feature Polar Bear $2 coins with a doubled die obverse.

Dollar coin doubling

While the coin has not been certified by any grading service, _Coin World_ has physically examined an example of the set containing the error. _Coin World_ News Editor William T. Gibbs identified the Loon dollar as probably showing Class IV Offset Hub Doubling. _Coin World’s_ Varieties Notebook columnist John Wexler agreed with that conclusion, after inspecting a digital image of the coin.

The Loon dollar exhibits doubling that is shifted in the same direction, the identifying characteristic of Class IV Offset Hub Doubling, which means the hub to die alignment was offset to one side. This type of doubling can occur with single-press hubbing, which was first used for Canadian coins in 1978.

Doubling is perhaps most visible in the words CANADA and DOLLAR and the designer’s initials on the reverse of the coin, which displays the standard Loon dollar design by Robert Ralph-Carmichael.

Trees at the water’s edge also exhibit doubling, and doubling is seen at the left wall of the incuse circle in which the maple leaf security device is found.

Wexler initially believed the doubling on the Loon dollar to be mechanical doubling, but closer inspection “shows a strong notching effect on many of the letters. The doubling on the beads near the rim does appear to be raised and rounded as does the doubling on other fine details such as the small trees and the designer’s initials.”

The final initial in the designer’s initials shows very nice separation of images, he added.

Class I doubling, like that on the famous 1955 Lincoln, Doubled Die Obverse cent, would give a notably different appearance than what is seen on the Loon dollar in the set.

Doubling on $2 coin

Less severe doubling is visible on the $2 coin, especially so in the word ELIZABETH, the year 2013 and the designer’s initials on the shoulder of Susanna Blunt’s effigy of Queen Elizabeth II.

The class of doubling on the $2 coin appears to be the same as on the Loon dollar, Wexler said.

The two coins illustrated with this article are in the same sealed set sold by the Royal Canadian Mint.

Discovery, RCM response

Variety collectors and some Canadian collectors first noticed the doubling back in March, based on online collector forum postings.

Cameron Giesbrecht, director of numismatics at Winnipeg’s Gatewest Coins, alerted _Coin World_ on Aug. 16, a few weeks after an unnamed customer of Gatewest tipped him off about the doubling.

Christine Aquino, director of communications at the Royal Canadian Mint, said the RCM was not aware of the doubling on the coins in the Uncirculated sets, though there was a general “understanding that this is a defect that can occur from time to time.”

The RCM has not located the die or dies responsible for striking the doubled coins, and could not provide an estimate of the possible numbers of pieces produced and released.

The set has a maximum mintage of 75,000 sets. Examples of the sets remained available Aug. 29 through the RCM website for the official issue price of $24.95 Canadian.

Examples of the Loon dollar with the doubling have sold through auction site [www.ebay.com](http://www.ebay.com/) for between $25 and $30, a price that die variety specialist Wexler noted was “quite a bargain” for such a “major variety.” ¦

## **Lucky loonie mintage plunges to record low in 2013**

**A review of mintage figures for 2013 suggests that some modern coins may prove difficult to find.**

While collectors often await the mintage figures in the Royal Canadian Mint’s (RCM) annual report, this year, Canadian Coin News looked at the figures over the past 10 years, and found that 2013 could be a year to watch in some denominations. Of particular interest are the higher value $1 and $2 coins, produced before the composition and design change introduced partway through 2012. For instance a 2013-dated $2 coin or a lucky loonie may be harder to find than that elusive de Salaberry 25-cent piece. Mintages for that year were updated in the 2013 report.

The RCM’s report did explain that mintages for last year were down from the previous year, and in most cases the drop was substantial.

The higher value coins saw a slight change in composition during the year to accommodate the RCM’s new plating plant, while at the same time new micro-engraving features were added including edge lettering the $2 coin.

The number of original pattern $2 coins produced in 2012 was a mere 1,531,000, down from 22,488,000 the year before, and the lowest reported in the last decade. It was also the last year for that composition. The new type $2 may be a tough find with the 2013 date, just 12,390,000 were produced, compared to 82,862,000 new-style coins produced in 2012. In the previous decade the lowest mintage was 22,488,000 in 2011 and the highest was 38,957,000 in 2007.

There is more balance in the case of the $1 coin. In 2012 the RCM manufactured just 2,414,000 old-pattern coins and 107,105,000 new-pattern coins. In 2013 a further 120,330,000 new-style loonies were struck. The lucky loonie struck in 2013 had it lowest mintage ever, just 969,000; the lowest mintage ever for the circulating coin. In the last 10 years the highest loonie mintage was 38,048,000 in 2007 and 20,410,000 in 2011.

High mintage figures for $1 and $2 coins in 2013 were expected, as the RCM’s alloy recovery program was culling the older composition coins out of circulation during the year.

The number of 50-cent coins produced, almost entirely for the collector market, was up in 2013 to 375,000 compared to 250,000 the year before. In 2010, the lowest year in the survey period, the mintage was 150,000.

Caribou pattern 25-cent pieces also saw a lower than usual mintage. In 2013 a total of 68,498,000 coins were produced, compared to 153,450,000 the year before. A further 12,500,000 each of the de Salaberry and Laura Secord coins were struck in 2013. The highest number in the past 10 years for the Caribou 25-centwas a whopping 423,189,999 in 2008, while the lowest was 20,446,000 in 2009.

The 2013-dated 10-cent coins set a new 10-year record, with just 104,775,000 compared to 334,675,000 in 2012. The highest in the period was 467,495,000 in 2008.

The humble five-cent coin, now the lowest-value coin in production, may be another tough find, with another record low posted in 2013. Last year just 78,120,000 nickels were produced, the lowest recorded since the coin shifted to a plated composition. The cupro-nickel version of the coin did see a lower mintage of 43,008,000 in 2008. Those coins were an irregularity, produced long after the RCM had shifted to plated coins, in order to compensate for a supply shortage of tri-plated blanks for five-cent coins.

Although not produced in 2013, the updated figures in the report show that 87,972,000 copper-plated zinc pennies were made in 2012, the lowest recorded over the past decade. The highest was 30,525,000 in 2005. The copper-plated steel coins were much more common. In 2012 a total of 111,375,000 were produced, the lowest figure in the past 10 years. The highest mintage was reported at 1,062,275 in 2006.

The total number of coins produced does not tell whole story of Canadian circulating coins.

Once made in Winnipeg, coins are shipped to 12 coin distribution centres across Canada based on local demand. Once in a centre, coins are then shipped to financial institutions or directly to high-volume users.

In the previous year, all coin centres ordered some inventories of each circulating coins, but some ordered relatively small numbers, making those coins harder to find in some parts of the country than in others.

The lowest demands were: five cent, St. Johns, N.L., 318,000; 10 cents, Quebec City, Que., 2,000; 25 cents, Halifax, N.S., 594,000; $1, St. John, N.B., 86,000; and $1, Halifax, 165,000.

The RCM distribution report simply records the number of coins shipped in a calendar year, and does not make any record on the commemorative designs or the years on the coins, so the distribution numbers can only be used as relative guides.

All circulating coin numbers in RCM annual reports are rounded to the nearest thousand.

## **Lucky loonie mintage plunges to record low in 2013**

**A review of mintage figures for 2013 suggests that some modern coins may prove difficult to find.**

While collectors often await the mintage figures in the Royal Canadian Mint’s (RCM) annual report, this year, Canadian Coin News looked at the figures over the past 10 years, and found that 2013 could be a year to watch in some denominations. Of particular interest are the higher value $1 and $2 coins, produced before the composition and design change introduced partway through 2012. For instance a 2013-dated $2 coin or a lucky loonie may be harder to find than that elusive de Salaberry 25-cent piece. Mintages for that year were updated in the 2013 report.

The RCM’s report did explain that mintages for last year were down from the previous year, and in most cases the drop was substantial.

The higher value coins saw a slight change in composition during the year to accommodate the RCM’s new plating plant, while at the same time new micro-engraving features were added including edge lettering the $2 coin.

The number of original pattern $2 coins produced in 2012 was a mere 1,531,000, down from 22,488,000 the year before, and the lowest reported in the last decade. It was also the last year for that composition. The new type $2 may be a tough find with the 2013 date, just 12,390,000 were produced, compared to 82,862,000 new-style coins produced in 2012. In the previous decade the lowest mintage was 22,488,000 in 2011 and the highest was 38,957,000 in 2007.

There is more balance in the case of the $1 coin. In 2012 the RCM manufactured just 2,414,000 old-pattern coins and 107,105,000 new-pattern coins. In 2013 a further 120,330,000 new-style loonies were struck. The lucky loonie struck in 2013 had it lowest mintage ever, just 969,000; the lowest mintage ever for the circulating coin. In the last 10 years the highest loonie mintage was 38,048,000 in 2007 and 20,410,000 in 2011.

High mintage figures for $1 and $2 coins in 2013 were expected, as the RCM’s alloy recovery program was culling the older composition coins out of circulation during the year.

The number of 50-cent coins produced, almost entirely for the collector market, was up in 2013 to 375,000 compared to 250,000 the year before. In 2010, the lowest year in the survey period, the mintage was 150,000.

Caribou pattern 25-cent pieces also saw a lower than usual mintage. In 2013 a total of 68,498,000 coins were produced, compared to 153,450,000 the year before. A further 12,500,000 each of the de Salaberry and Laura Secord coins were struck in 2013. The highest number in the past 10 years for the Caribou 25-centwas a whopping 423,189,999 in 2008, while the lowest was 20,446,000 in 2009.

The 2013-dated 10-cent coins set a new 10-year record, with just 104,775,000 compared to 334,675,000 in 2012. The highest in the period was 467,495,000 in 2008.

The humble five-cent coin, now the lowest-value coin in production, may be another tough find, with another record low posted in 2013. Last year just 78,120,000 nickels were produced, the lowest recorded since the coin shifted to a plated composition. The cupro-nickel version of the coin did see a lower mintage of 43,008,000 in 2008. Those coins were an irregularity, produced long after the RCM had shifted to plated coins, in order to compensate for a supply shortage of tri-plated blanks for five-cent coins.

Although not produced in 2013, the updated figures in the report show that 87,972,000 copper-plated zinc pennies were made in 2012, the lowest recorded over the past decade. The highest was 30,525,000 in 2005. The copper-plated steel coins were much more common. In 2012 a total of 111,375,000 were produced, the lowest figure in the past 10 years. The highest mintage was reported at 1,062,275 in 2006.

The total number of coins produced does not tell whole story of Canadian circulating coins.

Once made in Winnipeg, coins are shipped to 12 coin distribution centres across Canada based on local demand. Once in a centre, coins are then shipped to financial institutions or directly to high-volume users.

In the previous year, all coin centres ordered some inventories of each circulating coins, but some ordered relatively small numbers, making those coins harder to find in some parts of the country than in others.

The lowest demands were: five cent, St. Johns, N.L., 318,000; 10 cents, Quebec City, Que., 2,000; 25 cents, Halifax, N.S., 594,000; $1, St. John, N.B., 86,000; and $1, Halifax, 165,000.

The RCM distribution report simply records the number of coins shipped in a calendar year, and does not make any record on the commemorative designs or the years on the coins, so the distribution numbers can only be used as relative guides.

All circulating coin numbers in RCM annual reports are rounded to the nearest thousand.
